## Two Questions

This course presses on two questions.

1. What is rational choice when the unknowns are the actions of other rational agents?
2. What does it mean for a group to choose?

We will spend roughly half the semester on each.

## Question One

What is rational choice when the unknowns are the actions of other rational agents?

In standard decision theory, the things you are uncertain about are passive. The weather, the bus schedule, whether a coin will land heads. They do not react to what you are doing.

But many of the choices we care about involve other people, who are themselves trying to choose well, and whose choices depend on what they think you will do.

## A Coordination Problem

Two friends agree to meet at a café in Ann Arbor but did not say which. Both prefer Lab Cafe to Espresso Royale, and both prefer meeting somewhere to not meeting.

|       | Lab  | ER   |
|-------|------|------|
| Lab   | 3, 3 | 0, 0 |
| ER    | 0, 0 | 2, 2 |

What should each friend do?

## What Makes It Hard

Lab looks like the right answer: higher payoff if they coordinate there.

But that reasoning only works if each friend believes the other will reason the same way. And believes that the other believes that. And so on.

Rational choice in strategic settings has this iterated belief structure built in.

## The Prisoner's Dilemma

A different sort of puzzle.

|           | Cooperate | Defect |
|-----------|-----------|--------|
| Cooperate | 3, 3      | 0, 5   |
| Defect    | 5, 0      | 1, 1   |

Each player has a dominant strategy: defect, regardless of what the other does. So two rational players both defect. Both get 1, when both could have gotten 3.

## Why It Stings

There is a sense in which the players have done what each had reason to do. There is also a sense in which they have collectively failed.

We will see versions of this puzzle in many forms throughout the course. The point for now is just that "what does rationality recommend?" can be hard to answer even in very simple games.

## What the Game-Theory Half Will Do

Different proposed constraints on rational belief about other rational agents give different solution concepts.

The ones we will work through: Nash equilibrium, rationalizability, subgame perfection, sequential and perfect Bayesian equilibrium, and refinements like the Cho-Kreps intuitive criterion.

We finish with signaling games and applications to lemons markets (Akerlof) and labor markets (Spence).

## Question Two

What does it mean for a group to choose?

Different individuals have different preferences. Can we combine those preferences into a single group preference? When can we say what the group has decided?

This is a different question from Question One. The puzzle is aggregation rather than strategy.

## Condorcet's Paradox

Three voters, three options. Each column is a voter's ranking, top to bottom.

| Voter 1 | Voter 2 | Voter 3 |
|---------|---------|---------|
| A       | B       | C       |
| B       | C       | A       |
| C       | A       | B       |

Pairwise majority:

- A vs B: A wins, 2–1
- B vs C: B wins, 2–1
- C vs A: C wins, 2–1

The group "prefers" A to B to C to A. The group's preference is intransitive even though each individual's preferences are transitive.

## Generalizations

Condorcet noticed this in the 1780s. Arrow's theorem (1951) shows that no method of aggregating preferences can satisfy a small set of attractive conditions. Sen (1970) showed that you cannot combine a minimal commitment to individual liberty with even the weakest Pareto principle.

The puzzle: individually rational preferences do not always combine into a coherent group preference, and we want to understand why, and what to do about it.

## What the Social-Choice Half Will Do

We work through Amartya Sen's *Collective Choice and Social Welfare* (2017 expanded edition), the canonical philosophical treatment of aggregation.

Topics include Arrow's theorem with proof, Sen's Paretian liberal, interpersonal comparison and welfarism, equity and justice, the rights literature, and the capability approach.

## The Unifying Theme

The two questions look different. But the puzzle in each case has the same shape:

> Individual rationality does not extend cleanly to social settings.

Game theory and social choice theory are two different ways of seeing how, and what philosophers have made of it.

## Course Shape

Lectures 1–14 (through October 15): game theory.

Lectures 15–28 (October 22 through December 10): social choice, working through Sen.

Lecture 15, the first meeting after Fall Break, doubles as a transition lecture.

## Mathematical Level

Philosophy courses sometimes shy away from formal material. This one will not.

The mathematics will be at roughly the level of formal work in a philosophy journal. You should expect sets, functions, probabilities, expected utilities, and some algebra. Calculus will not be needed.

If you have taken Phil 305 or a similar course in formal methods, you should be comfortable. If you have not, ask questions; the formalism is there to make the structure visible.

## Required Reading

One required book: Amartya Sen, *Collective Choice and Social Welfare: An Expanded Edition* (Harvard University Press, 2017). Available electronically through the U-M library.

Game theory readings will be a mix of lecture notes, classic papers (Akerlof on lemons, Spence on signaling, Cho and Kreps on the intuitive criterion), and selected textbook chapters. Specific assignments will appear on Canvas.
